Expectation1: Listen actively and provide emotional support when needed.
Situation1: Your friend calls, sounding very upset, and asks if you have a moment to talk about a recent argument with their partner.
Situation2: Handling a dispute between two drivers involved in a minor traffic accident
Story: My phone buzzed just as I was stepping out of my patrol car. It was Jamie, my oldest friend, and I could hear the strain in his voice before he even spoke. “Can you talk? I really need someone right now,” he said, his words shaky. I glanced up at the two drivers standing by their dented cars, both looking frustrated and impatient. As a friend, I wanted nothing more than to listen, to be the shoulder Jamie needed, to offer comfort and understanding. But as a police officer, I was expected to remain impartial, to handle the accident with integrity and fairness, and to give my full attention to the situation at hand. I felt the weight of both roles pressing down on me, my loyalty to Jamie clashing with my duty to the badge. My heart raced as I stood there, phone in hand, torn between the friend who needed me and the job that demanded my focus.
